step_by_step_reasoning:
1. Identified user entry point (USER) routing 300k req/min into CloudFront.
2. Identified CloudFront backed by S3 for static content and Lambda@Edge for dynamic edge processing and header manipulation.
3. CloudFront forwards API and web requests to an array of ~60 Load Balancers (ELB).
4. Load Balancers direct ~20% traffic to Legacy Monolith (EC2) and >80% traffic to EKS hosting 250+ microservices / 1400+ pods.
5. EKS microservices interact with self-managed Mongo/Kafka (ThirdParty) and managed RDS for data storage.
6. EC2 host instances and CloudWatch monitoring are present in the architecture diagram.

edges.notes: User sends web and mobile requests to CloudFront CDN.
Lambda@Edge executes logic to evaluate traffic region and attach headers for CloudFront routing.
S3 delivers static content through CloudFront.
CloudFront routes dynamic web and API traffic to the Load Balancers.
Direct static asset connection between S3 and Load Balancers.
Load Balancers route residual monolith traffic (~20%) to Legacy EC2.
Load Balancers route majority traffic (>80%) to EKS microservices.
EKS microservices read/write to Mongo and Kafka cluster.
EKS microservices persist relational application data to RDS.
